title: Plan your retreat
hookLine: a day, a weekend or ten days: plan one for this coming year

lines: ONLY THE ONE WHO BRINGS FOOD.
HE COMES BACK AND TELLS THEM.
cards: Once, the Buddha told his monks he wanted to go into seclusion for three months, and that no one should come to him except the one who brought his alms food. The monks agreed. Three months went by.
When he came out, he told them how he had spent most of that time: mindful of the breath, in and out. The teacher of the whole community took time away.
He planned it, he told people, and he came back and said what he did there. That's a retreat. Today, with the year's practice traditions nearly done, plan your retreat.

teach.b: That story is in the Connected Discourses, in the chapter on breathing. It gives a retreat its shape: a set time, a protected space, a plain practice, and a return. Retreat is woven through Buddhist life.

teach.h: VASSA: STAY PUT FOR THE RAINS.
teach.b: The monks' rains retreat, the vassa, began in the Vinaya with a simple rule: during the rainy season, stay put in one place.

teach.h: A DAY, A WEEKEND OR TEN DAYS.
teach.b: Tradition makes that season a stretch of deeper practice, and lay people may join in, coming to the monastery on moon days. Earlier on this path you met what a retreat is, and sesshin, the Zen week of silence.
In some meditation centers today, people sit for ten days in silence. But a retreat doesn't have to be long. A day of mindfulness at home counts.
So does a weekend at a monastery that welcomes guests. What makes it a retreat isn't the length.

It's the four things from the Buddha's three months: a time you decide on in advance, a space protected from ordinary demands, one plain practice, and a way back. The planning isn't a chore before the real thing.
In the Buddha's story, telling the monks was part of it: someone knew where he was and who would bring the food.
The practices of these past weeks, chanting, bowing, pilgrimage, the perfections, the moon days, all live more deeply on a retreat. So today's step is small and practical. Not go now.

teach.h: WHEN, WHERE, HOW LONG, WHO KNOWS.
teach.b: Just know: when, where, how long, and who will know.

how: Buddhists go on retreats of a day, a weekend or longer at monasteries and meditation centers; monks keep the vassa, the rains retreat, and lay people may join it on observance days.

o: a set time, a protected place, one practice and a way back
a vacation spent resting, with no practice at all
leaving home for good to live as a monk in a monastery

games.q: plan your retreat: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha never took time away from his monks
in the Connected Discourses he goes into seclusion for three months, and tells them first.
a retreat has to be long to count
a day at home or a weekend counts; what matters is the time, the space, the practice and the way back.
the vassa began as a rule to stay in one place during the rains
in the Vinaya, the monks stay put for the rainy season.

games.q: you're the Buddha, about to go into seclusion. what do you do first?
o: tell the monks, and let only the one who brings food come.
take the whole community with you.
games.why: he tells them, they agree, and when he comes back he tells them he spent the time mindful of the breath.

practice: Sit for a few breaths the way the Buddha spent his three months: just the breath, in and out.

Then let a plan take shape: when you could step away this year, a Saturday, a long weekend, ten days; where, your own room with the phone off, a nearby temple, a center that runs retreats; what one practice you'd keep there, and who you'd tell.
Hold the four answers lightly, as if in pencil.

wordCard.voice: Plan your retreat. A set time, a protected place, one plain practice and a way back, decided before you go, as the Buddha did. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali vassa (Sanskrit varsha): the rains, and the rains retreat monks keep each year.

carryVoice: Your line: plan it. Even a single Saturday counts. I'll be here tomorrow.
